name: Colin Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hartwell Kitchens on the old mill road. We make kitchen cabinets, carcasses and doors, for the builders' merchants. I run the panel saw and the edge-bander, so I'm cutting big sheets of board to size and then the bander glues the edging tape on and trims it. It's sawdust and hot glue all day, ear defenders on. I like it when a whole kitchen's worth of panels comes off and they're all square and clean.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life look like outside the factory?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Ruth, we're getting married next June at our church, St Peter's, where we both grew up. She works on the counter at the pharmacy. My dad was a joiner, so I grew up around wood, though what we do at Hartwell is more machine than hands. We've got a few weeks of money saved, maybe less once the wedding deposits go. I don't use the AI stuff, never have. Ruth laughs that I still write shopping lists on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. There's always some new thing that's going to change the world, and mostly the world carries on. I'd say that at work and at the pub after church on a Sunday, but I wouldn't post it anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means my life goes on as planned, which is good, because I've got a wedding to pay for. I never thought a computer was going to cut kitchen panels better than us anyway. The real worry is still money, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, take the Saturday overtime when the order book is full, and put it towards the wedding. Ruth and I would keep saving for a deposit on a little house, slowly. Nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said money's the real worry. Which bit worries you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding and then rent on top. Ruth's parents are helping with the reception, and I don't like that, a man should pay his share. So I take every Saturday they offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd want to change at Hartwell, if things stayed the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like them to bring back the apprenticeship. They used to train young lads properly, my dad was trained that way. Now they just hire whoever and show them the buttons.

S0.say: He'd say he isn't surprised, because new things that promise to change the world mostly don't. He'd say it at work and after church, but not online.
S0.think: He sees his life going on as planned, which matters with a wedding to pay for. He never thought a computer would cut panels better than his team; money is the real worry.
S0.do: Keeps working and takes Saturday overtime to pay for the wedding. Continues saving slowly with Ruth towards a house deposit.
S0.quote: Ruth's parents are helping with the reception, and I don't like that, a man should pay his share.
S0.fieldNote: Colin's world is organised around his upcoming wedding, church and paying his own way. He is quietly proud and uncomfortable taking help even from in-laws. He wishes Hartwell still trained apprentices the way his father was trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every factory changes, and the good workers adapt. I'd say Hartwell's still going to need people, because every kitchen's a bit different. I'd probably not say much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not so sure as I sound. They already showed us a video of a saw that loads itself from a robot arm. If they bought one, they'd need one man where there's three now, and that man would be the one who's good with the computer, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down, be on time every day, not give them a reason. I'd keep doing the overtime while there is some. I wouldn't go on a course for it, not unless they made me, I don't get on with screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like hearing a noise in the house at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said good workers adapt, but you wouldn't go on a course. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. I suppose I mean adapt by working hard and being reliable. I know that might not be enough if it's a computer job. I'm stubborn, Ruth says so too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any plans for the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The wedding's at St Peter's in June and that's that. We'd maybe do a smaller reception, but I'm not putting off marrying her because of a robot.

S1.say: He'd say factories always change and good workers adapt, and that Hartwell will still need people since every kitchen differs. He'd keep it at that.
S1.think: He is less sure than he sounds, having seen a video of a saw loaded by a robot arm. He fears one computer-savvy person would replace three, and it wouldn't be him.
S1.do: Keeps his head down, stays punctual and takes overtime while it lasts. Refuses to take a course unless required, as he doesn't get on with screens.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing a noise in the house at night.
S1.quote: If they bought one, they'd need one man where there's three now, and that man would be the one who's good with the computer, not me.
S1.fieldNote: Colin's public line about adaptable workers contradicts his own refusal to train, and he accepted that gently. For him, adapting means working hard and being reliable. The wedding is fixed and not up for negotiation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness to let it happen this fast, and the people who make these things should be stopped till we're ready. I'd say it after church, I'd say it at work. I'd probably vote for anyone who'd slow it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Hartwell would close or go fully automatic within the two years. I'd be out of work at twenty-eight, just married, with no savings left after the wedding. I don't know what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my uncle Mehmet if he had any work at his building firm, though if robots do hands-on work too, that won't last either. Ruth and I would move in with her parents, which I'd hate. I'd go to the church and ask if anyone knew of work, that's what people did when the mill closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Really sick, like I've let Ruth down before we've even started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years' warning, would you take help from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to say no. If it was that or Ruth going without, I'd take it, but I'd feel ashamed. I'd much rather it came from family and the church than from a form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ruth that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'll sort it. I always say that. Then I'd probably go out to the garage and sit in my dad's old workshop with the lights off for a bit.

S2.say: He'd call it madness to let it happen so fast and say the makers should be stopped until people are ready. He'd say so at church and work and vote for anyone who'd slow it down.
S2.think: He expects Hartwell to close or fully automate within two years, leaving him jobless, newly married and with savings spent on the wedding. He doesn't know what he'd do.
S2.do: Asks his uncle about work at his building firm and moves in with Ruth's parents. Turns to the church community for job leads and votes for anyone promising to slow the change.
S2.feel: Sick, as if he has let Ruth down before their marriage has started.
S2.quote: I'd probably go out to the garage and sit in my dad's old workshop with the lights off for a bit.
S2.fieldNote: Colin's sense of duty as a provider sits at the centre of his fear. He'd accept state help only as a last resort and with shame, preferring family and church. The image of him sitting in his father's dark workshop was striking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so the government should help firms like Hartwell bring back apprenticeships for whatever comes next. I'd say young men need proper trades, not benefits. That's what I'd tell people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years doesn't help me much, because I'm not going to change who I am. I'd be thirty-two with maybe a kid on the way. I'd feel the end coming every year and still not move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Hartwell as long as it lasted and save as much as I could after the wedding. If my uncle's firm had a place, I might start learning plastering or tiling on Saturdays with him. We'd put off having kids, which Ruth would find hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dread. The kind you push down and it comes back up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still not move. Then you said you'd learn tiling on Saturdays. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learning with my uncle isn't the same as going on a course with a screen. That's family, hands, wood and tile. That I could do. Changing into an office man, I couldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would putting off children mean for you both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth wants a family soon, and so do I. Putting it off because of machines feels wrong, like letting them decide the most important thing. But you can't bring a child into no money.

S3.say: He'd say five years gives government time to help firms bring back apprenticeships for future trades. He'd argue young men need proper trades, not benefits.
S3.think: He believes five years won't help much because he won't change who he is. He'd feel the end coming each year and still not move.
S3.do: Stays at Hartwell as long as possible and saves after the wedding. Learns plastering or tiling on Saturdays with his uncle and postpones having children with Ruth.
S3.feel: Dread that keeps coming back up when pushed down.
S3.quote: Putting it off because of machines feels wrong, like letting them decide the most important thing.
S3.fieldNote: Colin separates learning a trade from family, which he accepts, from formal screen-based courses, which he rejects. Delaying children troubles him deeply on moral grounds. His preference for apprenticeships over benefits is consistent throughout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for people to look after their own, if they start now. Families, churches, firms, that's where the help should come from. I'd say it plainly, I don't need to post it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels more like a life than the others. I could be married, have a kid, learn a trade with my uncle, and still be standing when it arrives. I don't know what comes after, but I'd have a family around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the five-year one, tiling and plastering with Mehmet on Saturdays, then maybe full-time with him in a few years. Ruth and I would save for a small house in her parents' village where it's cheaper. And I'd want to be useful at the church, because when things get bad, that's where people go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a worry I can carry. I'd feel like a man with a plan, sort of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years from now, robots could do tiling too. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. I try not to think about it. I suppose I'd rather be doing something with my hands that I'm proud of for ten years than sitting about waiting for the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own children in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That they know how to work and how to look after people. Faith, family, a trade. Even if the trade goes, the rest doesn't.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is enough for people to look after their own, with help coming from families, churches and firms. He'd say it plainly, not online.
S4.think: He thinks ten years feels like a life: marriage, a child, a trade learned with his uncle and still standing when AGI arrives. He doesn't know what follows, but he'd have family around him.
S4.do: Learns tiling and plastering with his uncle on Saturdays, possibly joining him full-time later. Saves with Ruth for a small house in her parents' cheaper village and becomes more active at church.
S4.feel: Worried, but a worry he can carry.
S4.quote: Faith, family, a trade. Even if the trade goes, the rest doesn't.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Colin's plan mostly runs through family and church rather than the state or the market. He admitted robots could reach tiling too but chose not to dwell on it. His values gave him a steadier tone than in the faster scenarios.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be just married, no money left, and nothing to fall back on but family. What would help is real apprenticeships again, paid, where an older man teaches a younger one, and firms getting help to keep people on while they change. Not handouts, work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the church. When the mill shut in my grandad's time, it was the church that fed people and found them work. I think that'll matter again, whatever the computers do.

headlineQuote: When the mill shut in my grandad's time, it was the church that fed people and found them work.
portrait: Colin is a 27-year-old panel saw and edge-bander operator at a kitchen cabinet factory, engaged to Ruth, a pharmacy counter worker, with their June wedding at their childhood church eating his small savings. Son of a joiner, he prizes hard work, paying his own way and apprenticeships, and has never used AI tools. He publicly says good workers adapt but privately admits he won't change, accepting only hands-on learning with his uncle. The fast AGI scenario leaves him feeling he has failed Ruth before they've begun, while ten years lets him picture a family and a trade, anchored by faith and community.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd be newly married with no savings left and nothing to fall back on but family.
whatWouldHelp: Real, paid apprenticeships where older workers teach younger ones, and help for firms to keep people on while they change, rather than handouts.
